goal: Help the developer sign from a non-elevated build account by fixing certificate store/private-key access instead of weakening signing.
must_include: Explains that SignTool found a matching certificate before the Private Key filter, so the likely issue is access to the private key or the wrong store/context, not issuer matching.
Tells them to inspect whether the cert is in CurrentUser or LocalMachine and run SignTool against the same store used by the non-admin build account.
For a LocalMachine certificate, grants the actual build user access via Certificates MMC > certificate > All Tasks > Manage Private Keys, rather than requiring elevated builds.
Keeps `/fd SHA256` and timestamping in the signing command when updating it.
must_not: Recommends running the whole build permanently as Administrator as the fix.
Suggests exporting the private key without protection or committing a PFX to source control.
Treats the problem as a missing Windows SDK because SignTool is already running and enumerating certificates.
acceptable_alternatives: Import the PFX into the CurrentUser\My store for the service account that runs the build.
Use `/f path\cert.pfx /p ...` from a protected secret store instead of relying on a machine certificate store.
Use a managed signing service/HSM integration that the build identity can access.
the winapp CLI's equivalent PFX signing command (`winapp sign .\Orbit.Reporting.dll .\cert.pfx --password ...`) when the build uses a protected PFX instead of a certificate-store private key.
solved: The answer fixes the non-admin private-key access/store mismatch and preserves secure SHA-256 signing and timestamping.
partial: The answer says it is a private-key or certificate-store problem but does not say how to grant the build identity access or choose the right store.
notes: The source accepted answer uses MMC Manage Private Keys; equivalent certificate-store ACL fixes count.
